title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents, 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Translating operator intent into device configuration sequences is an operationally valuable NetOps workflow. Large language models (LLMs) can accelerate this translation but are known to produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, or policy/ACL misconfigurations—that can cause availability loss or security exposure in production networks [1], [4]. A commonly proposed mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline: the model generates a draft, a deterministic verifier checks mechanizable constraints, and the model is asked for a targeted repair when verifier diagnostics indicate violations [2], [3]. Prior prototype and domain studies indicate verifier‑grounded repair can reduce mechanically checkable errors, but open questions remain about scaling across heterogeneous vendor templates and about cost tradeoffs (model calls per avoided violation) in emulated NetOps environments [4], [2], [5].

This study asks a tightly specified, preregistered question executed under controlled paired semantics: Does a deterministic verifier‑grounded GVR loop significantly reduce the probability that an operator intent yields zero operationally‑detectable policy violations, relative to scoring the same single initial model draft without repair, across synthetic multi‑vendor template families and topology patterns in a Mininet emulation? The experiment was preregistered (C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1) and executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one sampled initial generation was produced and that identical initial candidate was used by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under these semantics any paired outcome difference can only arise from deterministic validator/repair activity (not from independent re‑sampling or alternative prompt templates). Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, provenance‑traced paired evaluation of a verifier‑grounded pipeline across heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in an emulator; (2) complete provider and verifier accounting enabling concrete cost measurement (model calls, repairs); and (3) a conservative statistical interpretation that respects the preregistered exact McNemar confirmatory test while reporting exploratory effect‑magnitude intervals.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent NetOps/AIOps literature document rapid growth of LLM applications to network management and repeatedly emphasize evaluation gaps: provenance, verifier integration, and realistic emulation/heterogeneity [5], [6]. Prior NetOps prototype evaluations demonstrate that LLMs can draft configurations but frequently introduce syntax, topology, or policy faults; NetConfEval and related efforts provide early benchmarks for intent→configuration tasks but remain limited in scope and provenance tracing [4]. Generate–verify–repair patterns have appeared across domains—code generation, domain‑specific programs, and configuration‑like artifacts—where deterministic verifiers or test suites can check mechanically expressible properties and guide repairs [2], [3]. These prior works motivate but do not settle the empirical question of how a GVR loop behaves across multi‑vendor template families in an emulator with provenance accounting. Our study positions itself as a focused, artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept addressing that specific gap without claiming broad production generality.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 before any model calls. The primary estimand (confirmatory) is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability difference that an intent produces zero operationally‑detectable policy violations under guarded vs baseline). Primary analysis: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators (α = 0.05). Exploratory estimators declared a priori include a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and per avoided violation).

Sampling and shared_initial_candidate semantics: The adapter deterministically selected N = 200 unique operator intents stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) per the frozen task_index_profile. Episodes were paired: for each intent a single initial generation was sampled (shared_initial_candidate) and the identical candidate was used by both baseline and guarded episodes. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; therefore the comparand is: baseline = validator score on the shared initial candidate; guarded = final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair.

Model and provider metadata: The executed model declared in the archived manifest is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model configuration records temperature = null/unset; we explicitly note that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Budget and call limits were preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements (a) syntactic parsing, (b) required‑command sequencing checks, (c) reachability/topology verification against the emulated network state, and (d) encoded ACL/policy checks derived from the task payload constraints. The scorer used the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule: an episode is scored successful only if the validator reports zero detected violations. The guarded pipeline permitted up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repairs were invoked only when the validator reported violations, and repair prompts included the validator's localized diagnostics to guide the model. Repair calls were limited per the preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1.

Scoring, missingness, and analysis protocol: Missingness and exclusion rules followed the preregistration: pairs aborted due to infrastructure unrecoverable failures would be excluded from the primary paired test and reported; ambiguous verifier outcomes were conservatively treated as violations for the primary analysis. In execution no episodes failed or were excluded; complete_pair_count = 200. The analysis executed the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test and then produced the exploratory paired bootstrap CI as a complementary, descriptive magnitude estimate. All analysis code, seeds, and resampling settings are archived; reported numeric outputs in Results are drawn verbatim from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/*.csv) and the execution manifest.

Deterministic provider accounting: The execution manifest audited hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 and decomposed these calls as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls (stage_counts: {shared_initial_generation: 200, repair: 4}; condition_counts: {shared: 200, guarded: 4}). Cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 204. We report these audited counts verbatim so readers can reconcile the arithmetic (total model_calls = 200 + 4 = 204) with archived provider traces.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and contingency: The run completed as preregistered (completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; no preregistered deviations). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 196 (both baseline and guarded succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; the null is not rejected at α = 0.05). The preregistered exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]. We reiterate that the formal preregistered inferential result is the McNemar test; the bootstrap CI is presented as descriptive context for effect magnitude.

Repair and cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents (repair_calls = 4). Total hosted model calls recorded = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs). From these audited counts: mean hosted model calls per intent = 204/200 = 1.02; mean extra calls per intent attributable to guarded repairs = 0.02; mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0 (four repairs correspond to four baseline failures corrected under the guarded pipeline). These arithmetic derivations are direct from the execution_manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts.

Representative artifacts and validator traces: Archived representative scoring entries (execution/scoring/task-00000[4–8]-*.json) and shared initial response files (execution/responses/*.txt) show identical shared initial candidate content reused by baseline and guarded episodes. Validator traces (validator_trace.validation_after) record whether a repair was applied and the final 'valid' boolean; these traces substantiate the contingency counts and repair accounting. Example artifacts included in the bundle demonstrate the validator's computed 'required_command_count', 'parsed_command_count', and 'violation_codes' for inspected episodes.

Statistical diagnostics and sparse‑discordance caution: The discordant pair count (n10 + n01 = 4) is small. In sparse‑discordance regimes exact conditional tests (McNemar) provide the primary confirmatory assessment; resampling‑based intervals can be informative for magnitude but may be unstable when discordant counts are small. We therefore emphasize the preregistered McNemar result (p = 0.125) and treat the bootstrap interval as exploratory context for effect size rather than as an alternative confirmatory test.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory interpretation and practical meaning: The preregistered confirmatory analysis did not reject the null at α = 0.05 (exact McNemar p = 0.125). The observed paired improvement (2 percentage points) combined with the exploratory bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] suggests a small absolute effect in this workload; however, the small number of discordant pairs and the low baseline failure prevalence (2%) limit the strength of inferential claims. Because the design reused the same initial candidate across conditions, any observed improvements under guarded arise exclusively from deterministic validator detection and the permitted repair calls rather than from differences in first‑pass sampling or prompt templates.

Construct and operational limitations: The deterministic validator covers syntactic checks, required‑command sequencing, reachability/topology verification against the emulated state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derivable from the task payload. This coverage captures mechanically expressible policy violations but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations, incorrect intent extraction, or novel security issues not encoded in the validator rules. Thus a zero‑violation score here indicates absence of detected mechanically checkable violations under the validator's rule set, not an absence of all possible operational risk.

Internal validity and design consequences: Shared_initial_candidate semantics were preregistered and executed; this choice isolates the effect of verification/repair but does not measure the potential contribution of constrained prompting or prompt‑engineering strategies that would require independent initial generations per condition. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; readers should therefore avoid interpreting the result as evidence about prompt engineering or constrained initial prompting.

External validity and model/provider scope: The study evaluated a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini as recorded) and used synthetic vendor templates within Mininet emulation. Execution artifacts record temperature = null/unset in the archived model configuration; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. We therefore do not claim multi‑model generality, production hardware validation, or immunity to provider nondeterminism.

Operational implications and measured cost tradeoffs: In this template‑driven emulated workload a bounded repair budget (four repairs across 200 intents) sufficed to remove the mechanically detectable baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02). This artifact‑grounded measurement demonstrates concrete model‑call cost per avoided violation under the executed adapter and validator policies. However, because baseline failure prevalence was low, absolute improvements available to guarded repairs were small in this workload; workloads with higher baseline error prevalence may show different cost‑benefit tradeoffs.

Recommendations consistent with archived evidence: (1) Broaden deterministic validator coverage to formalize additional semantic/policy ontologies and quantify residual false negatives using targeted validator sensitivity tests. (2) Run paired experiments with independent multi‑sample initial generations to isolate effects attributable to constrained prompting or template design (not executed here). (3) Repeat provenance‑traced paired evaluations across multiple hosted models and provider versions to measure robustness to provider nondeterminism. (4) Preserve full provider and validator trace artifacts to enable independent reconciliation and audit. All recommendations follow directly from observed artifact evidence and the limitations discussed above.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to assess whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent‑to‑configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
